what_its_for: Ketoprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve mild to moderate pain, reduce fever, and decrease swelling and stiffness caused by conditions like arthritis (including rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis), menstrual cramps, and other types of pain.
how_to_take: Take ketoprofen exactly as directed by your doctor or as stated on the package label. Always take it with a full glass of water (8 ounces). Take it with food, milk, or an antacid to help protect your stomach and reduce the chance of an upset stomach. Do not lie down for at least 10 minutes after taking this medicine. Swallow extended-release capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or break them open.
dosing: The usual adult dose for pain relief is 25 mg to 50 mg taken every 6 to 8 hours as needed. For arthritis, your doctor may prescribe 150 mg to 300 mg per day divided into smaller doses. The maximum dose is generally 300 mg per day for prescription strength. For over-the-counter use, do not take more than directed on the label (usually 12.5 mg to 25 mg every 4 to 6 hours). Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you are taking ketoprofen on a regular schedule and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ketoprofen at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medications down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of them.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking ketoprofen, as it increases your risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin) at the same time unless your doctor tells you to. Avoid taking ketoprofen if you are allergic to aspirin or other NSAIDs. Do not take more than the recommended dose. Avoid prolonged sun exposure, as ketoprofen may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Talk to your doctor before taking any new prescription or over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice: black, tarry, or bloody stools; vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds; severe stomach pain; chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurred speech (signs of a possible heart attack or stroke); swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; skin rash, blistering, or peeling; sudden weight gain or swelling in your legs or ankles; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); decreased or no urination; or severe headache or vision changes. Also call your doctor if your pain or fever does not improve or gets worse after a few days.
when_it_works: Ketoprofen usually starts working within 30 minutes to 1 hour after you take it. You may feel pain relief fairly quickly, but it may take a few days to a few weeks of regular use before you experience the full benefit for conditions like arthritis.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Use with extra caution. Older adults are at a higher risk for stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart-related side effects. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time possible. Pregnant women: Do not use ketoprofen during the last 3 months of pregnancy (third trimester), as it can harm the unborn baby. Talk to your doctor before using it in early pregnancy. Breastfeeding mothers: Talk to your doctor before using ketoprofen, as it may pass into breast milk. Children: Ketoprofen is generally not recommended for children unless specifically prescribed by a doctor. People with kidney or liver disease: Use with caution and only under close medical supervision, as ketoprofen can make these conditions worse.
